extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in journalism/media studies and linguistics; scholars studying news values, news selection and news discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesis and evaluation of criteria (news values/factors) used to determine newsworthiness and to analyse how events/stories/images are selected and constructed as news. Includes conceptual distinctions (material/cognitive/discursive), methodological guidance, and lists of specific news-value dimensions from major authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: the time-span needed for the event to unfold and the match between event frequency and the news medium's frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘the more similar the frequency of the event is to the frequency of the news medium, the more probable that it will be recorded as news by that news medium’ (used to explain likelihood of broadcast/print coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold (absolute intensity, intensity increase)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: the intensity or size of an event (absolute magnitude or sharp increase) that makes it newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher intensity or a marked increase raises the probability of selection; sometimes operationalised as magnitude/impact in later lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: clarity of interpretation—events with clear, single meanings are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘an event with a clear interpretation, free from ambiguities in its meaning, is preferred to the highly ambiguous event’; linked to news writing objectives like simplification and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness (cultural proximity, relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: cultural closeness or relevance of an event to the audience increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also expressed elsewhere as proximity or relevance; culture-bound vs culture-free distinctions discussed in the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance (predictability, demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: the extent to which an event fits expected themes/patterns of news (theme predictability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps explain why some events are picked because they 'fit' existing narratives or expectations; relates to composition and news agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (unpredictability, scarcity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: novelty or surprise in an event increases likelihood of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also labelled Novelty/Unusualness/Surprise in many later taxonomies; often combined with human interest or drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: events that continue an ongoing story or theme are more likely to remain news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to follow-up and frequency; once something is in the news it tends to stay there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: how an event/story fits within the overall set of stories (balance and programme composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors aim for mixture and balance; composition affects selection by making some items useful to ‘fit’ larger story packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge (culture-bound): presence or reference to powerful countries increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of ‘elite’ related factors; used to explain geographical/cultural priorities in foreign news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite people
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge (culture-bound): involvement or mention of elite/important people raises a story's news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later taxonomies use Prominence/Eliteness/Celebrity, with near-identical definitions across authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge (culture-bound): human-centredness/personalisation makes events more newsworthy than abstract processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the privileging of people in news and the role of personalization/identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to something negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge (culture-bound): negativity, harm or bad outcomes increase news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matches many later lists' emphasis on negativity, conflict, bad news and drama as strong drivers of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity Hypothesis (Galtung & Ruge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis that 'the higher the total score of an event, the higher the probability that it will become news, and even make headlines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an analytic assumption in factor-based studies (cumulative effects), though originally not empirically tested by Galtung & Ruge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity Hypothesis (Galtung & Ruge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis that low score on one news factor must be compensated by a high score on another complementary factor for selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests trade-offs between factors; has guided subsequent studies testing interactions among values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence / Eliteness / Celebrity / Status
rubrics_metrics.description: A widely-cited news value: involvement of elite people, organisations or celebrities increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various labels (Prominence, Worth, Power); definitions across 11+ authors are almost identical — eliteness of actors or nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity / Bad News / Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories featuring harm, damage, controversy, violence or negative developments tend to be highly newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes conflict/dramatization, damage, violence/aggression; often measured as valence (negative/positive/neutral) in coding schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact / Magnitude / Significance-Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an event affects people/audiences (consequence, significance, scale) increases news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed as Impact, Consequence, Significance; central to assessing why floods, disasters, policy changes are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Recency or topicality of an event: the more current or immediate, the higher its newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial for news photos and breaking news; linked to frequency and the news cycle (mediatisation of time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical, cultural or psychological nearness of an event to the audience increases news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local topics predominate in photos and stories; cultural proximity also encompassed under Meaningfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest / Personalization / Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that provide a human face, emotions or personalization are perceived as more newsworthy and memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses emotional/entertaining or touching aspects; often traded against elite-focused stories to create balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment / Picture opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment value and the availability of visually attractive images (picture opportunities) can drive selection even when intrinsic newsworthiness is low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup & O'Neill note picture opportunities often lead to inclusion; Brighton & Foy and others include entertainment as a standard value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Unusualness / Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking, rare or unexpected aspects of an event increase newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combined with human interest or spectacle; labelled Unexpectedness in Galtung & Ruge, Unusualness or Surprise by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition / Balance / Story-mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors seek a balanced package across subjects, geographies and moods; how a story fits the broader programme/page matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps explain selection for variety and internal fit (e.g., finishing bulletins with human-interest items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity / Simplification / Clarity / Brevity (news writing objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic objectives — clarity, simplicity, brevity and the reduction of ambiguity — make items more suitable for news formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are both stylistic production values and selection-relevant criteria; important for broadcast where time/space is constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that can be followed up over time (continuity) or that build on previous coverage are more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to continuity and the news barrier; once a story is set it becomes easier to publish related items.

rubrics_metrics.name: News agenda / Newspaper agenda / Agenda fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit a news organisation’s editorial agenda are prioritized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial priorities, thematic agendas and 'stories that set the organisation's agenda' shape selection beyond standalone event qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: External influences / Competition / Organisational requirements / Commercial pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Market orientation, budgets, competition for exclusives, proprietorial and advertiser pressures affect selection and what counts as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Østgaard, Allern and others highlight internal/external constraints (news sources, cost, editorial policy) as selection factors distinct from news values per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual attractiveness / Picture opportunity (photography-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: For images: availability of dramatic/attractive film or photos makes a story more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographic selection often privileges timeliness, proximity and drama; techniques like colour, contrast and perspective affect 'execution and technique'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic technique / Execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographic quality — colour, contrast, light, perspective and dramatic effort — influences the news value of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rössler et al. and others note execution is a criterion beyond event-properties; good technique can elevate otherwise weak items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source / Availability of images or ready-made text (prefabrication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of ready-made material (photos, agency copy, press releases) increases likelihood of coverage due to ease and deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as part of the news barrier concept; availability often driven by press releases and agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict / Dramatization (visual and textual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of conflict, tension or drama in an event or image raises its newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News photos typically embody tension; conflict often central in award-winning news imagery and front-page stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (positive news representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of positive or uplifting elements can influence whether and how events are visually represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some evidence that positive stories are more often represented visually to entertain or divert; considered alongside negativity in valence coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization in images (emotions, showing people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images that concretize issues through people, emotions and identifiable faces increase memorability and news appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press photos tend to feature working/middle class people rather than elites; 'emotions' is a codable visual news factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality / eroticism (visual factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual or erotic content can function as a distinct attractor in image selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among visual-specific values (Craig 1994, Rössler et al.) as an occasionally decisive factor for inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core international values: Interest, Timeliness, Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton's proposed three-element core of newsworthiness: Interest, Timeliness and Clarity — regarded as minimal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masterton suggests these are accepted internationally as core values without which information cannot become news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material / Cognitive / Discursive perspectives on news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual distinction: (a) material perspective — newsworthiness in the event's material reality; (b) cognitive perspective — journalists' beliefs/judgements about what is newsworthy; (c) discursive perspective — how texts (language, photography) construct newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend reserving 'news values' for newsworthiness while distinguishing these perspectives; useful for choosing analytic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational measurement methods (content analysis, ethnography, coding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods used to study news values: content analysis (coding presence/absence, interval scales, placement/length), ethnography (interviews, newsroom observation) and multi-method approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content analysis is prevalent but limited for explaining selection motives; coding schemes include presence/absence of elites, valence, picture opportunities, intensity scales and placement metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donsbach's four decision-influencing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Donsbach proposes four main influences on journalists' decisions: news factors, institutional objectives, manipulative power of news sources, and subjective beliefs of journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful framework for including psychological and organisational determinants when analysing selection beyond event properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: News barrier / Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal production constraints and simplification processes that make some items 'pass the news barrier' (simplicity, identification, excitement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described by Østgaard and others; includes factors like ready-made text, ease of reporting, and editorial selection thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamics: Timeliness, Facticity, Suspense, Secrecy, Uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal and product-related dynamics affecting newsworthiness: timeliness, degree of factual detail, suspense (open questions), secrecy (revealed information), and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'other' factors map onto audience engagement drivers (suspense) and informational richness (facticity) used in coding and theorising news value.
